claims.text: Single-phase fcc FeCoNi or an fcc FeCoNi-based derivative has high saturation magnetization and coercivity no greater than 100 Oe.
The proposed intervention is addition of 2–5 at% Ti to an fcc FeCoNi-based alloy.
An FeCoNi-based alloy containing 2–5 at% Ti can remain within the high-entropy fcc regime.
Adding 2–5 at% Ti will form coherent nanoscale Ti-rich precipitates or induce lattice distortions in the fcc matrix.
The Ti-rich precipitates or lattice distortions will act as magnetic domain-wall pinning centers.
Inhibition of domain-wall motion by these pinning centers will increase coercivity.
The Ti addition and resulting microstructure will largely preserve the alloy's high saturation magnetization.
The Ti-modified alloy could exhibit more than twice the baseline coercivity and exceed 200 Oe.
Composition and synthesis parameters can affect nanoscale decomposition or feature dimensions and the resulting magnetic-property balance.
The relevant structural boundary is an fcc matrix without extensive multiphase decomposition beyond nanoscale precipitates.
Coercivity and saturation magnetization should be measured at room temperature using VSM hysteresis loops.
TEM and XRD can be used to assess precipitate formation, size, distribution, and lattice or phase structure.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis requires retention of a single-phase fcc structure while also proposing and attempting to confirm Ti-rich precipitates. Compositionally distinct precipitates normally constitute an additional phase, so the permitted structural state is not defined consistently unless the mediator is limited to lattice distortions or coherent compositional fluctuations.

The numerical criteria are not equivalent. For a baseline anywhere at or below 100 Oe, a factor-of-two increase is not necessarily greater than 200 Oe, and failure to double is not equivalent to coercivity remaining at or below 100 Oe.
